newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-RBNZ not seeking easier actual conditions.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-RBNZ not seeking easier actual conditions.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand in its Monetary Policy Statement on Friday said it was not seeking any further easing in actual monetary conditions.
However, it said there may be some scope for a further small easing in monetary conditions in the December quarter.

The inflation projections outlined in the bank's MPS assumed monetary conditions would be the equivalent of 100 basis points easier during the September quarter than the conditions assumed in the March economic projections.
"This new level of desired monetary conditions is in fact very close to where actual monetary conditions have been in recent weeks," RBNZ Governor Don Brash explained.
"In other words, we are not seeking any further easing in actual monetary conditions."
The bank said it now believed that the economy grew more slowly in the first two quarters of 1997 than it thought likely when it issued its March Economic Projections.

"Indicators for the March quarter in particular suggest that there was quite an abrupt slowing during the first three months of the year. Indeed, it is not inconceivable that the economy may even have contracted slightly in that quarter," Brash said.

"Indicators for the June quarter, however, along with our own business contacts, suggest that the economy may have rebounded somewhat in that quarter, and we currently project that growth will strengthen in subsequent quarters."
Brash said that beyond the end of 1997, the bank saw the need for monetary conditions to remain broadly stable in inflation-adjusted terms.

"This maintenance of monetary conditions at a reasonably firm level relates to our expectation that the economy will have only minimal excess capacity available by mid-1998, when further tax cuts and increased government spending take effect."

Brash said that as "a very approximate guideline", the RBNZ expected actual monetary conditions to be within a range of plus or minus 50 MCI points from desired in the week's immediately following a comprehensive inflation projection.

The RBNZ said the main argument that could be made for a more significant easing of conditions than presented in its projections was that inflation was seen falling below the centre of the target range for much of the next year or two.
However, a number of factors suggested a more cautious approach. If the exchange rate passthrough remained lower than the bank expected, inflation in the short term would be higher than projected.

The RBNZ did not expect a large margin of excess capacity to emerge in the economy. A sharper easing of conditions in the short term would leave the economy with little spare capacity with which to absorb the stimulus from easing, tax cuts and higher government spending.
The bank also said if activity weakened by more than it projected, the downward risk to inflation would be less than the upward risk to inflation if activity proved more resilient than projected.
